title: State transportation exposure is non-monotonic across median-income quartiles
source_unit: 2024 ACS state/DC/PR aggregate tables B08201, B08303, and B19013
geography: United States states, District of Columbia, and Puerto Rico

denominator.unit: pooled state households for vehicle measure; pooled workers 16+ not working from home for commute measure

observations.method: States sorted into four equal-count groups by B19013 median household income; B08201 and B08303 estimates pooled within quartile using their table totals. Commute 30+ combines B08303_E008 through B08303_E013.
observations.uncertainty: No margin-of-error propagation is calculated; state aggregate estimates have sampling and nonsampling error. Quartiles are state-level contextual groups, not household-income groups.
observations.subgroup: 13 geographic rows with median household income from $27,213 to $72,212.
observations.counterinterpretation: The lowest-income state group has lower long-commute exposure than higher groups, so vehicle scarcity and commute time do not form a single monotonic burden scale.

denominator.unit: pooled state households for vehicle measure; pooled workers 16+ not working from home for commute measure

observations.method: Same state-quartile pooling method as quartile 1.
observations.uncertainty: No margin-of-error propagation is calculated; state aggregate estimates have sampling and nonsampling error. Quartiles are state-level contextual groups, not household-income groups.
observations.subgroup: 13 geographic rows with median household income from $72,350 to $77,735.
observations.counterinterpretation: A state median-income context does not identify who can afford transport, who has alternatives, or whether long commutes are chosen or required.

denominator.unit: pooled state households for vehicle measure; pooled workers 16+ not working from home for commute measure

observations.method: Same state-quartile pooling method as quartile 1.
observations.uncertainty: No margin-of-error propagation is calculated; state aggregate estimates have sampling and nonsampling error. The quartile includes high-density places whose vehicle scarcity can raise the pooled share.
observations.subgroup: 13 geographic rows with median household income from $77,871 to $87,534.
observations.counterinterpretation: The higher no-vehicle share may reflect dense urban form and transit availability rather than greater unmet mobility; the aggregate tables do not identify mode quality or trip success.

denominator.unit: pooled state households for vehicle measure; pooled workers 16+ not working from home for commute measure

observations.method: Same state-quartile pooling method as quartile 1.
observations.uncertainty: No margin-of-error propagation is calculated; state aggregate estimates have sampling and nonsampling error. State median income is a context variable and not a household resource measure.
observations.subgroup: 13 geographic rows with median household income from $92,090 to $109,707.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher-income states can have longer commutes without lower welfare if wages, transit, housing choice, or schedule control offset time; none are observed here.

boundary: This is a state-context comparison, not a household-income gradient or causal estimate. B19013 ranks geographic contexts; B08201 and B08303 are aggregate tables with different universes. The result does not establish affordability, transit quality, care access, missed activity, or political response. The detailed state rows and source hashes are reproducible through the companion analysis script.
